results.note: SoF 2 and (a) 2nd paragraph match. Analysis 1.2 forest plot: 13/75 v 43/73 events (Batey, Benos, Yu); 43/73 = 589 per 1000, x 0.32 = 188.
SoF 2 and (d) 1st paragraph match. Analysis 1.3 forest plot: 41/75 v 21/73 completed; 21/73 = 288 per 1000, x 1.95 = 562 (SoF 561).

results.corrected_extracted: Sedation and dry mouth about twice as common with clonidine as with placebo (Benos 1985); drowsiness and dizziness in 7 of 16 on clonidine against 0 of 15 on placebo (Batey 1987); with lofexidine against placebo, blood pressure fell, hypotension 18% against 0% and insomnia 42% against 9%, and 4 of 35 against 0 of 33 stopped treatment for adverse effects (Yu 2008).
results.note: Numbers right; the Yu clause did not name placebo. Not carried: Benos judged these effects troublesome in only a few cases; in Batey none withdrew for adverse effects.
Matches. The forest plots of Analyses 1.2 and 1.3 do name the three trials (16+15, 24+25, 35+33 = 148); Benos enrolled 50, one excluded after randomisation. 'Fentanyl' appears nowhere in the review.
SoF and Intensity of withdrawal paragraphs 1 to 3 match, including grades (low: bias and few events; moderate: few participants). Peak score P = 0.07; severe withdrawal P = 0.39.

results.corrected_extracted: In all eight trials that described the time course, withdrawal signs and symptoms appeared earlier and resolved sooner with an alpha2 agonist; with tapered methadone, withdrawal in general peaked late, at the end of the taper.
results.note: First clause right. The review hedges the methadone point (in general; five trials cited) and places the peak at the end of the taper.

results.corrected_extracted: Time in treatment shorter with an alpha2 agonist than with reducing doses of methadone: SMD -1.07 (-1.31 to -0.83), 3 trials, 310 participants, GRADE low; SMD -1.04 (-1.44 to -0.64) without the high-risk trial.
results.note: Numbers and grade right; only the comparison group added. The excluded high-risk trial is Jiang 1993 (110 participants remain).

results.corrected_extracted: Hypotensive or other adverse effects, alpha2 agonist against reducing doses of methadone: RR 1.92 (1.19 to 3.10), 6 trials, 464 participants, GRADE low; illustrative 79 per 1000 with methadone against 151 per 1000 with an alpha2 agonist; without the three high-risk trials RR 2.02 (0.62 to 6.64), 203 participants. Drop-out for adverse effects RR 3.62 (0.77 to 16.94), 4 trials, 153 participants, no events in methadone arms. In one trial 89 of 100 people on clonidine had dizziness on standing.
results.note: Numbers right; adds the comparison and labels the illustrative arms. Without the three high-risk trials the difference was no longer significant.

results.corrected_extracted: Completion, alpha2 agonist against reducing doses of methadone: RR 0.85 (0.69 to 1.05), 9 trials, 659 participants, GRADE low (selection bias, heterogeneity); illustrative 568 per 1000 with methadone against 483 per 1000 with an alpha2 agonist; without San 1990 RR 0.91 (0.75 to 1.11). People withdrawing from heroin RR 0.87 (0.61 to 1.25); from methadone RR 0.97 (0.80 to 1.18); inpatient RR 0.87 (0.68 to 1.12), I2 67%; outpatient RR 1.09 (0.73 to 1.64).
results.note: Numbers right. Adds the comparison, labels the illustrative arms, and makes clear the heroin and methadone subgroups are the opioid people were withdrawing from.

Kahn 8/14 (57%) v 13/14 (93%); Lin 25/615 (4.1%) v 45/508 (8.9%) occasions; no meta-analysis for this comparison. Lin also reported no clinically significant hypotension (pressures down about 10 mmHg in both groups).

results.corrected_extracted: Neither alpha2 agonists nor a methadone taper appeared to fully suppress aches and pains, sleep disturbance, loss of energy, chills or anxiety. The authors note that fixed methadone tapers in the trials, unlike flexible tapers in practice, would be expected to bias the comparison against methadone.
results.note: Restores the review's hedges: neither treatment appears to suppress these fully, and inflexible tapers are a potential bias expected to disfavour methadone, said of all included trials (blinding is one reason).

results.corrected_extracted: Completion of withdrawal treatment, buprenorphine against clonidine or lofexidine: RR 1.59 (95% CI 1.23 to 2.06), 11 trials (12 comparisons), 1264 participants, GRADE moderate (heterogeneity above 60%); illustrative 453 per 1000 with clonidine or lofexidine against 721 per 1000 with buprenorphine; number needed to treat for one additional completion 4 (2.8 to 6.7); inpatient RR 1.74 (1.05 to 2.89), 539 participants; outpatient RR 1.45 (1.12 to 1.88), 725 participants.
results.note: Numbers right; the illustrative risks were unlabelled and in the reverse order of the named comparison. NNT 4 (2.8 to 6.7) is from Results; the abstract gives 3 to 6.

results.corrected_extracted: Mean overall withdrawal score lower with buprenorphine than with an alpha2 agonist in all seven trials reporting it: SMD -0.43 (-0.58 to -0.28), 902 participants, GRADE moderate (blinding of subjective outcomes); without four high-risk trials SMD -0.37 (-0.58 to -0.16).
results.note: Numbers and grade reason right; adds the comparison group. Excluded trials: Hussain 2015, Ling 2005, Lintzeris 2002, Nigam 1993.

results.corrected_extracted: Time in treatment longer with buprenorphine than with clonidine: SMD 0.92 (0.57 to 1.27), 4 trials (5 comparisons), 558 participants, GRADE moderate; large in both inpatient and outpatient settings.
results.note: Numbers right; adds the comparison group as the text names it (clonidine; the one lofexidine trial did not report duration). Scheduled durations differed, hence the SMD.

results.corrected_extracted: Any adverse effect, buprenorphine against an alpha2 agonist: RR 0.93 (0.70 to 1.26), 3 trials (4 comparisons), 493 participants, GRADE very low; stopping for adverse effects only in clonidine arms, RR 0.20 (0.04 to 1.15), 3 inpatient trials, 134 participants, low. Dizziness, dry mouth and lethargy typical with clonidine; headache, constipation and nausea with buprenorphine.
results.note: Numbers right; adds the comparison. Nigam also reported constipation with clonidine. Uncited 4th paragraph: serious adverse events in Ling 2005 outpatients 14/157 on buprenorphine (10 substance use or overdose) v 4/74 on clonidine.
Matches the 2nd paragraph; the review does not say which intervention showed the benefit.

results.corrected_extracted: Completion, buprenorphine against methadone: RR 1.04 (0.91 to 1.20), 5 trials, 457 participants, GRADE moderate (small number of participants); illustrative 528 per 1000 with methadone against 549 per 1000 (481 to 634) with buprenorphine.
results.note: Numbers right. SoF 1 footnote b gives the downgrade as a small number of participants (N < 300), although 457 took part; 'fewer than 300 events' is SoF 2's footnote wording.

results.corrected_extracted: Mean days in treatment, buprenorphine against methadone: MD 1.30 days (-8.11 to 10.72), 2 trials, 82 participants, GRADE low (different settings, small numbers).
results.note: Numbers right; adds the comparison (SoF: 1.3 days more with buprenorphine). Methadone-group means were 10.8 or 48.5 days, so the two trials differed widely.

Matches paragraphs 1 to 5 and the adverse-effects paragraph: Petitjean day 8 v days 13 and 16; Seifert days 8 and 14 (graphs only); Steinmann 2008 and Wright 2011 did not report; Bickel, Seifert, Umbricht.
Matches: Umbricht 2003 in an AIDS service, Wright 2011 in a prison healthcare centre, Bickel 1988 the only outpatient trial.
Matches Results, SOWS Total Peak Scores. The abstract gives days 2-5 for the self-rated elevation, Results days 2-6; the anchor follows Results. F(1,6) as printed.
Severe-range percentages for days 2-5 and no difference on days 1 and 7 match; symptom list matches the text and Table 2 footnote (yawning and urge to use had no cohort main effect).

results.corrected_extracted: Peak observer-rated withdrawal higher in the Fentanyl than in the Non-Fentanyl cohort from the second to the seventh day (F(1,6) = 7.76, p < 0.001). No participant reached moderately severe or severe COWS scores; mild observer-rated withdrawal, Fentanyl against Non-Fentanyl cohort, 73% against 33%, 70% against 13%, 73% against 18%, 60% against 15%, 53% against 18% and 40% against 14% on those days.
results.note: Numbers right; adds the comparison group and the order of the percentages. Abstract gives days 2-6, Results days 2-7.

results.corrected_extracted: Tachycardia (heart rate above 100 at least once) in 43% of the Fentanyl cohort against 19% of the Non-Fentanyl cohort (p < 0.05); heart rate rose more steeply over the week in the Fentanyl than in the Non-Fentanyl cohort (interaction p = 0.007).
results.corrected_locator: Methods › Measures, 2nd paragraph; Results › Physiological Measures › Heart Rate, 1st paragraph
results.note: Numbers right; adds the comparison group. The 'at least once' definition is in Methods; Results print '>1 incidence'. No main effect of cohort on heart rate (P = 0.416).

results.corrected_extracted: The Fentanyl cohort was older than the Non-Fentanyl cohort (mean 46.0, SD 10.1, against 41.2, SD 10.2; p = 0.021). Concomitant medicines for withdrawal symptoms were available during stabilization only in the Fentanyl trial, because of uncontrolled withdrawal.
results.note: Table 1: 46.03 (10.11) v 41.17 (10.24), P 0.021; adds the comparison group. Medicines were given after each rating timepoint; no other demographic differed.
All seven limitations are in the 5th Discussion paragraph (the paper spells nitazenes as nitazines); it adds that standard rating protocols should mitigate observer bias.

plain.fix: how[0]: Three trials gave people coming off heroin either the medicine or a dummy pill, picked by chance.
plain.note: All three pooled trials enrolled heroin users (Yu 2008 excluded methadone and other long-acting opioids); 'heroin or methadone' is the review's wording for all six placebo trials. Batey 1987 did not state random allocation, though the review counts all trials as randomised. Other lines match SoF 2.

plain.fix: short: No clear difference in how many people finished, but clonidine-type medicines caused more low blood pressure and other side effects. | how[3]: Neither way seemed to take away all the aches, bad sleep and worry.
plain.note: Completion RR 0.85 (0.69 to 1.05), low certainty, 57 v 48 in 100: no significant difference, not equal numbers. The pooled harm is hypotensive or other adverse effects (dizziness is one trial). The review hedges the residual-symptom point.

plain.fix: but: No trial reported people coming off fentanyl, and two stopped early, which may have skewed the results. | how[2]: On buprenorphine, withdrawal was milder on average and people stayed in treatment longer than on the other medicines. | how[3]: There was no clear difference in how many had side effects, but they differed: headache with buprenorphine, dizziness and dry mouth with clonidine.
plain.note: The review never mentions fentanyl or dates the trials against it, and does not say which way early stopping biased results. Side-effect counts are very low certainty; the Discussion names headache for buprenorphine, and constipation occurred in both arms of one trial.
Matches SoF 1 (549 v 528 per 1000, moderate), the authors' view that the two appear equally effective with limited data, and the settings (four inpatient, one prison, one outpatient).

plain.fix: short: In one study, people coming off fentanyl had worse withdrawal than people coming off other opioids, such as heroin. | how[1]: Both groups got the same medicine on the same research ward, but only the fentanyl group could also get extra medicines for symptoms.
plain.note: The comparison cohort had non-fentanyl opioid exposure (e.g., heroin, oxycodone), not heroin only; the question could read 'heroin or other opioids'. Only the Fentanyl trial offered concomitant medicines during stabilization. Other lines match.
